aero-w1-q1.question: In which layer of the atmosphere does almost all weather (clouds, rain) occur, with temperature falling as height increases?
aero-w1-q1.explanation: The troposphere is the lowest layer (up to about 11 km). Almost all water vapour and weather is here, and temperature falls with height. Trap: temperature also falls in the mesosphere, but there is no weather there; the stratosphere holds the ozone layer and its temperature rises.

aero-w1-q2.question: In the ISA model, what is the temperature at 4 km altitude? (sea level 288.15 K, lapse rate 6.5 K/km)
aero-w1-q2.explanation: T = 288.15 − 6.5 × 4 = 288.15 − 26 = 262.15 K. Temperature falls as you climb in the troposphere. Trap: 314.15 K comes from adding the 26 K instead of subtracting it; 248.15 K from using a lapse rate of 10 K/km.

aero-w1-q3.question: At some altitude the pressure is 61,640 Pa and the temperature is 262.15 K. Taking R = 287 J/(kg·K) for air, what is the density?
aero-w1-q3.explanation: ρ = p/(RT) = 61,640 / (287 × 262.15) ≈ 0.819 kg/m³. Trap: putting pressure in kPa (61.64) gives 8.19 × 10⁻⁴, and using the universal constant 8.314 gives 28.3; 1.225 is only the sea-level value.

aero-w1-q4.question: An airliner cruises at 33,000 ft. Taking 1 ft = 0.3048 m, what is this altitude in km?
aero-w1-q4.explanation: 33,000 × 0.3048 = 10,058 m ≈ 10.06 km. Trap: dividing by 0.3048 instead of multiplying gives 108.3 km, which is above the atmosphere itself; always do a sanity check like this.

aero-w1-q5.question: A gas cell has a measured volume of 2.5 m³ and the air density is 1.225 kg/m³. How should the mass of air inside be written with correct significant digits?
aero-w1-q5.explanation: 1.225 × 2.5 = 3.0625, but 2.5 has only 2 significant digits, so the answer takes 2 s.f.: 3.1 kg. Trap: writing every calculator digit (3.0625) is false precision, and 3 kg keeps only 1 s.f.

aero-w1-q6.question: In the ISA troposphere, p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^5.256. At 11 km, T = 216.65 K, with T₀ = 288.15 K and p₀ = 101.325 kPa. What is the pressure at 11 km, approximately?
aero-w1-q6.explanation: T/T₀ = 216.65/288.15 = 0.752. (0.752)^5.256 ≈ 0.223, so p ≈ 0.223 × 101.325 ≈ 22.6 kPa. Trap: forgetting the exponent and using only the temperature ratio gives 76.2 kPa, and taking the exponent as 1/5.256 gives 96.0 kPa. Pressure falls much faster than temperature.

aero-w1-q7.question: From what height is space conventionally taken to begin (the Kármán line)?
aero-w1-q7.explanation: The Kármán line is taken at 100 km; in air that thin, getting lift from a wing would need nearly orbital speed. Trap: 11 km is the top of the troposphere, 50 km of the stratosphere and 85 km of the mesosphere; these are layer boundaries, not the start of space.

aero-w1-q8.question: What are the dimensions of pressure (force per unit area) in terms of M, L and T?
aero-w1-q8.explanation: Force = MLT⁻² and area = L², so pressure = MLT⁻²/L² = ML⁻¹T⁻². Trap: MLT⁻² is just force (the division by area was forgotten), ML²T⁻² is the dimension of energy, and ML⁻³ is density.

aero-w1-q9.question: A trainer aircraft is flying at 200 knots. Taking 1 knot = 0.5144 m/s, what is its speed in m/s?
aero-w1-q9.explanation: 200 × 0.5144 = 102.9 m/s. Trap: treating knots as km/h and dividing by 3.6 gives 55.6 m/s, and using the foot factor 0.3048 gives 61.0 m/s; dividing by 0.5144 gives 388.8 m/s, which is far too high.

aero-w1-q10.question: In the ISA model, what is the temperature in °C at an altitude of 9 km? (sea level 288.15 K = 15 °C, lapse rate 6.5 K/km)
aero-w1-q10.explanation: T = 288.15 − 6.5 × 9 = 288.15 − 58.5 = 229.65 K, and 229.65 − 273.15 = −43.5 °C. Trap: forgetting the 15 °C at sea level and just subtracting 58.5 gives −58.5 °C, using a 10 K/km lapse rate gives −75.0 °C, and writing the kelvin value as °C gives 229.65 °C.

aero-w1-q11.question: A student writes a term ρV² (density × velocity²) in a formula. What are its dimensions, and which quantity do they match?
aero-w1-q11.explanation: ρ = ML⁻³ and V² = L²T⁻², so ρV² = ML⁻³ × L²T⁻² = ML⁻¹T⁻², which is the dimension of pressure. Trap: adding the powers of L wrongly (taking −3 + 2 as +1 or +2) gives a force-like or energy-like answer; forgetting to square the velocity gives T⁻¹.

aero-w1-q12.question: Using the ISA model, find the air density at an altitude of 2 km. (T₀ = 288.15 K, p₀ = 101325 Pa, lapse rate 6.5 K/km, p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^5.256, R = 287 J/(kg·K))
aero-w1-q12.explanation: T = 288.15 − 13 = 275.15 K. T/T₀ = 0.9549, (0.9549)^5.256 ≈ 0.7846, so p ≈ 79,500 Pa. ρ = 79,500/(287 × 275.15) ≈ 1.007 kg/m³. Trap: putting T in °C (2 °C) gives 138.5, putting the pressure in kPa gives 1.007 × 10⁻³, and 1.225 is only the sea-level value.

aero-w1-q13.question: In the ISA troposphere, at what altitude will the pressure be 50,000 Pa? (T₀ = 288.15 K, p₀ = 101325 Pa, lapse rate 6.5 K/km, p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^5.256)
aero-w1-q13.explanation: p/p₀ = 50,000/101,325 = 0.4935. T/T₀ = (0.4935)^(1/5.256) ≈ 0.8743, so T ≈ 251.9 K. h = (288.15 − 251.9)/6.5 ≈ 5.57 km. Trap: taking the pressure ratio directly as the temperature ratio gives 22.5 km, treating pressure as linear between 0 and 11 km gives 7.17 km, and raising to the power 5.256 instead of 1/5.256 gives 43.2 km (outside the troposphere).

aero-w1-q14.question: An aircraft flies at 350 knots (3 significant digits) for 2.0 h (2 significant digits). Taking 1 knot = 0.5144 m/s, how would you write the distance covered in km with the correct significant digits?
aero-w1-q14.explanation: 350 × 0.5144 = 180.0 m/s; 2.0 h = 7,200 s; distance = 180.0 × 7,200 ≈ 1,296,000 m ≈ 1,296 km. The least precise input is 2.0 (2 s.f.), so 1.3 × 10³ km. Trap: 1296 km is false precision, 1.30 × 10³ has 3 s.f., and treating knots as km/h and doing 350 × 2.0 gives 7.0 × 10² km.

aero-w1-q15.question: On a hot day the pressure at an airport is 101325 Pa but the temperature is 35 °C. Taking R = 287 J/(kg·K), find the density, and how much lower it is than the ISA sea-level density (1.225 kg/m³).
aero-w1-q15.explanation: T = 35 + 273.15 = 308.15 K. ρ = 101325/(287 × 308.15) ≈ 1.146 kg/m³. 1.146/1.225 ≈ 0.935, about 6.5% lower; this is why the take-off run is longer on a hot day. Trap: taking the °C ratio (15/35) gives 57%, putting T = 35 (°C) gives 10.09 kg/m³, and assuming the same density just because the pressure is the same is wrong.

aero-w2-q1.question: A TV broadcast needs a satellite that always appears at the same spot from the ground, so home dishes never need to turn. Which orbit fits?
aero-w2-q1.explanation: A GEO satellite circles above the equator with the same period as Earth's rotation, so it looks fixed from the ground and a fixed dish works. Trap: 'sun-synchronous' also sounds synchronous, but it is synced with the Sun, not with Earth's surface; that satellite keeps moving across the sky.

aero-w2-q2.question: Which of these roles belongs to military aviation rather than civil aviation?
options: Refuelling fighters in the air (aerial refuelling tanker)
Spraying pesticide on farms with a drone
aero-w2-q2.explanation: Air-to-air refuelling of fighters is a military mission that extends the range of combat aircraft. Passenger flights, air ambulances and crop spraying are all civil applications. Trap: assuming any drone is military; drones are widely used for civil work too.

aero-w2-q3.question: A GEO satellite is directly above a ground station at 35,786 km. How long does a signal take to go from the ground to the satellite and back to the ground (one hop)? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
aero-w2-q3.explanation: Total distance = 2 × 35,786 km = 71,572 km = 7.157 × 10⁷ m. Time = 7.157 × 10⁷/(3 × 10⁸) ≈ 0.24 s. Trap: 0.12 s is only one leg (going up), and 0.48 s is two hops (question and reply), which is what you notice in a phone call.

aero-w2-q4.question: A survey drone has a 111 Wh battery, of which only 80% may be used. The drone draws 300 W. What flight time does it get?
aero-w2-q4.explanation: Usable energy = 0.8 × 111 = 88.8 Wh. Time = 88.8 / 300 = 0.296 h = 0.296 × 60 ≈ 17.8 min. Trap: forgetting the 80% gives 22.2 min, and not converting hours to minutes gives 0.30; 3.38 h comes from dividing power by energy.

aero-w2-q5.question: Why is a sun-synchronous orbit often chosen for remote-sensing (imaging) satellites?
options: The satellite passes over a place at the same local solar time each time, so lighting stays nearly the same across images
The satellite looks fixed at one spot from the ground
This orbit is the farthest from Earth, so the whole Earth is visible at once
In this orbit the satellite never gets sunlight
aero-w2-q5.explanation: The plane of a sun-synchronous orbit turns in step with the Sun, so the satellite passes at the same local time on each pass and shadows and lighting stay comparable, which matters for detecting changes. Trap: looking fixed from the ground is a GEO property, not a sun-synchronous one.

aero-w2-q6.question: An airliner burns 2,400 kg of fuel per hour in cruise and flies at 800 km/h with 180 passengers. How much fuel per passenger does a 1,200 km cruise take? (cruise only, ignore other phases)
aero-w2-q6.explanation: Time = 1,200/800 = 1.5 h. Total fuel = 2,400 × 1.5 = 3,600 kg. Per passenger = 3,600/180 = 20 kg. Trap: 3,600 kg is the fuel for the whole aircraft, 13.3 kg is the per-passenger fuel for one hour only (the 1.5 h was forgotten), and 0.0167 kg is per passenger per km.

aero-w2-q7.question: What application is India's regional satellite system NavIC meant for?
aero-w2-q7.explanation: NavIC is India's regional navigation system; like GPS it gives position and time. Trap: remote sensing, weather and communication are also satellite applications, but NavIC's job is navigation.

aero-w2-q8.question: What is usually the biggest limitation of battery-powered drones?
options: Too much top speed and noise
The need for an on-board pilot
aero-w2-q8.explanation: A battery holds little energy, so flight time ≈ usable energy / power is the main limit. Trap: drones need no runway or on-board pilot, and too much speed is not their problem.

aero-w2-q9.question: From the system view, what does the design of a new aerospace vehicle start from?
options: The cheapest engine on the market
The paint and interior scheme of the last aircraft
A wing as large as can be built
aero-w2-q9.explanation: Every application starts from a mission requirement, and that decides the vehicle's type, size, propulsion and cost. Trap: the engine or wing size is chosen after the requirement, not before.

aero-w2-q10.question: A mapping drone has a 14.8 V, 5 Ah battery. Only 85% of the energy may be used and the drone draws 250 W. How long can it fly?
aero-w2-q10.explanation: Energy = 14.8 × 5 = 74 Wh; usable = 0.85 × 74 = 62.9 Wh. Time = 62.9/250 = 0.2516 h = 0.2516 × 60 ≈ 15.1 min. Trap: forgetting the 85% gives 17.8 min, reading 0.2516 h as 25.2 min gives 25.2 min, and treating Ah as Wh gives about 1.0 min.

aero-w2-q11.question: A LEO internet satellite is directly above a ground station at an altitude of 550 km. How long does a signal take to go from the ground to the satellite and back to the ground (one hop)? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
aero-w2-q11.explanation: Distance = 2 × 550 km = 1,100 km = 1.1 × 10⁶ m. Time = 1.1 × 10⁶/(3 × 10⁸) ≈ 3.7 × 10⁻³ s = 3.7 ms. Trap: taking only one leg gives 1.8 ms, a wrong km-to-m conversion gives 37 ms, and 0.24 s is the GEO delay, not LEO.

aero-w2-q12.question: Riya talks to Arjun on the phone through a GEO satellite (35,786 km, assume directly above both stations). After Riya asks a question, Arjun replies at once. What is the minimum delay before Riya hears the reply? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
aero-w2-q12.explanation: Question: ground → satellite → ground = 2 legs; reply: another 2 legs. Total 4 × 35,786 km ≈ 1.431 × 10⁸ m, time = 1.431 × 10⁸/(3 × 10⁸) ≈ 0.48 s. Trap: taking just one hop gives 0.24 s, just one leg gives 0.12 s, and counting the legs twice gives 0.95 s.

aero-w2-q13.question: A spraying drone has a 22.2 V, 5 Ah battery, only 80% of the energy may be used, and it draws 444 W. Spraying a field needs 55 min of flying in total. What is the minimum number of full battery charges needed?
aero-w2-q13.explanation: Energy = 22.2 × 5 = 111 Wh; usable = 88.8 Wh; time = 88.8/444 = 0.2 h = 12 min per battery. 55/12 ≈ 4.58, and part of a battery is not a whole flight, so 5. Trap: forgetting the 80% gives 15 min and 55/15 ≈ 3.67 → 4; rounding 4.58 down also gives 4; forgetting the 80% and rounding down gives 3.

aero-w2-q14.question: In cruise, airliner A burns 2,400 kg/h of fuel at 800 km/h with 180 passengers. Airliner B burns 3,000 kg/h at 850 km/h with 240 passengers. Which is better in fuel per passenger per 100 km?
options: A: it burns less fuel per hour
aero-w2-q14.explanation: A: 2,400/800 = 3 kg/km, ÷ 180 = 0.0167 kg per passenger-km → 1.67 kg per 100 km. B: 3,000/850 = 3.53 kg/km, ÷ 240 = 0.0147 → 1.47 kg. B is better. Trap: looking only at kg/h makes A look better, and ignoring speed to get kg per passenger-hour (12.5 vs 13.3) is not a per-km comparison.

aero-w2-q15.question: An aircraft must cruise 1,500 km at 900 km/h, burning 2,700 kg/h of fuel. On top, 45 min of reserve fuel (same burn rate) is needed. How much fuel must be loaded in total? (cruise and reserve only)
aero-w2-q15.explanation: Cruise time = 1,500/900 = 1.667 h; cruise fuel = 1.667 × 2,700 = 4,500 kg. Reserve = 0.75 h × 2,700 = 2,025 kg. Total = 6,525 kg. Trap: forgetting the reserve gives 4,500 kg, writing 45 min as 0.45 h gives 5,715 kg, and taking the time the wrong way round as 900/1,500 gives 3,645 kg.

aero-w3-q1.question: Which of these is an aerostat (lighter-than-air)?
aero-w3-q1.explanation: A hot-air balloon flies on the buoyancy of the hot, lighter air inside it, so it is an aerostat. The glider, helicopter and quadcopter are all heavier than air and fly on aerodynamic lift from a wing or rotor. Trap: a glider has no engine, but it still flies on wing lift.

aero-w3-q2.question: What is the main job of the tail rotor in a conventional helicopter?
options: Giving extra lift so more payload can be carried
Balancing the main rotor's reaction torque and giving yaw control
Blowing air to keep the engine cool
aero-w3-q2.explanation: When the engine turns the main rotor, the reaction torque tries to spin the helicopter body the other way. The tail rotor gives sideways thrust that balances this torque, and by changing that thrust the pilot controls yaw. Trap: forward thrust comes from tilting the main rotor forward, not from the tail rotor.

aero-w3-q3.question: A helium balloon has a volume of 600 m³. ρ_air = 1.225 kg/m³ and ρ_He = 0.169 kg/m³. What total mass (envelope + payload) can it lift?
aero-w3-q3.explanation: Net lift per m³ = 1.225 − 0.169 = 1.056 kg. Total = 1.056 × 600 ≈ 634 kg. Trap: 735 kg comes from forgetting to subtract the helium's own weight; 6,216 is really the force in newtons (634 × 9.81), so writing it in kg is a unit error.

aero-w3-q4.question: At sea level ρ_air = 1.225 kg/m³ (288.15 K) and ρ_He = 0.169 kg/m³. A hot-air balloon heats its air to 373.15 K (same pressure). For the same net lift, roughly how many times the volume of the helium balloon does the hot-air balloon need?
aero-w3-q4.explanation: ρ_hot = 1.225 × 288.15/373.15 ≈ 0.946, so the hot-air lift is 1.225 − 0.946 = 0.279 kg/m³. Helium lift is 1.056 kg/m³. Ratio = 1.056/0.279 ≈ 3.78. Trap: 1.30 is just the ratio of temperatures (or densities), not of net lift; 0.26 comes from taking the ratio upside down.

aero-w3-q5.question: A quadcopter has a mass of 1.5 kg (g = 9.81 m/s²). In steady hover, how much thrust must each motor give?
aero-w3-q5.explanation: Weight = 1.5 × 9.81 = 14.7 N. In hover total thrust = weight, shared equally by four motors: 14.7/4 ≈ 3.68 N. Trap: 14.7 N is the thrust of the whole drone; 7.36 N is needed for a thrust-to-weight of 2 (maximum thrust for manoeuvring), not for hover.

aero-w3-q6.question: A 1,000 m³ helium balloon can lift 1,056 kg at sea level (ρ_air = 1.225, ρ_He = 0.169 kg/m³). At 3 km ρ_air = 0.909 and ρ_He = 0.126 kg/m³. If the volume stays the same, what mass can it lift at 3 km?
aero-w3-q6.explanation: Net lift at 3 km = (0.909 − 0.126) × 1,000 = 783 kg. Both air and helium get thinner, so lift falls roughly by the air-density ratio (0.909/1.225 ≈ 0.74). Trap: assuming the same volume gives the same lift (1,056 kg); 1,099 kg comes from mixing the sea-level air density with the 3 km helium density.

aero-w3-q7.question: Which of these is an aerodyne (heavier-than-air)?
aero-w3-q7.explanation: A glider is heavier than air and gets lift from its wing, so it is an aerodyne. Trap: the airship and both balloons fly by gas buoyancy, so they are aerostats, even though the airship has engines.

aero-w3-q8.question: Hydrogen gives more lift than helium, so why do passenger airships and balloons today usually use helium?
options: Helium gives more lift when heated
Helium is inert and does not catch fire
aero-w3-q8.explanation: Hydrogen is the lightest but is flammable; helium gives slightly less lift but is inert and safe. Trap: helium is heavier than hydrogen, not lighter, and hydrogen is far lighter than air.

aero-w3-q9.question: What is the main difference between a balloon and an airship?
options: An airship flies only on hot air
An airship is steered with engines and fins
A balloon has propellers and a rudder
aero-w3-q9.explanation: Both are aerostats, but a balloon drifts with the wind (only up-down control), while an airship has engines/propellers and control fins. Trap: a balloon is lighter-than-air, and propellers/rudders belong to the airship, not the balloon.

aero-w3-q10.question: At sea level ρ_air = 1.225, ρ_He = 0.169 and ρ_H₂ = 0.085 kg/m³. If a 500 m³ balloon is filled with hydrogen instead of helium, how much extra mass can it lift?
aero-w3-q10.explanation: Helium: 500 × (1.225 − 0.169) = 528 kg. Hydrogen: 500 × (1.225 − 0.085) = 570 kg. Extra = 570 − 528 = 42 kg (that is, 500 × (0.169 − 0.085)). Trap: 570 kg is the total hydrogen lift, not the extra; 84 kg comes from doubling the difference, and 4.2 kg from a misplaced decimal.

aero-w3-q11.question: For good control, a 2 kg quadcopter should have total maximum thrust equal to 2 times its weight (g = 9.81 m/s²). What maximum thrust should each motor have?
aero-w3-q11.explanation: Weight = 2 × 9.81 = 19.62 N. Total maximum thrust = 2 × 19.62 = 39.24 N; each motor = 39.24/4 ≈ 9.81 N. Trap: 4.91 N is only the hover thrust (the factor of 2 was forgotten), 19.6 N comes from not dividing by 4 or writing just the weight, and 39.2 N is the total for the whole drone.

aero-w3-q12.question: A hot-air balloon must lift 500 kg (envelope + basket + people). The outside air is at 288.15 K (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) and the inside air is heated to 373.15 K (same pressure). What is the minimum envelope volume needed?
aero-w3-q12.explanation: ρ_hot = 1.225 × 288.15/373.15 ≈ 0.946 kg/m³. Lift per m³ = 1.225 − 0.946 = 0.279 kg. V = 500/0.279 ≈ 1,792 m³. Trap: using the °C ratio (15/100) gives 480 m³, taking the hot-air density itself as the lift gives 529 m³, and dividing by the outside density alone gives 408 m³.

aero-w3-q13.question: A 3,000 m³ hot-air balloon must lift 900 kg. Outside ρ_air = 1.225 kg/m³ and T = 288.15 K (same pressure). To at least what temperature must the inside air be heated?
aero-w3-q13.explanation: Lift per m³ = 900/3,000 = 0.3 kg, so ρ_hot = 1.225 − 0.3 = 0.925 kg/m³. ρ ∝ 1/T, so T_hot = 288.15 × 1.225/0.925 ≈ 381.6 K (about 108.5 °C). Trap: inverting the ratio gives 217.6 K (colder than outside), writing the °C value as K gives 108.5 K, and using 0.3 in place of ρ_hot gives 1,177 K.

aero-w3-q14.question: A quadcopter has a mass of 1.2 kg on its own and each motor gives a maximum thrust of 8 N (g = 9.81 m/s²). Following the rule that total maximum thrust should be 2 times the weight, what is the largest payload it can carry?
aero-w3-q14.explanation: Total maximum thrust = 4 × 8 = 32 N. Rule: weight ≤ 32/2 = 16 N, so total mass ≤ 16/9.81 ≈ 1.63 kg. Payload = 1.63 − 1.2 ≈ 0.43 kg. Trap: forgetting the 2-times rule gives 2.06 kg, forgetting to subtract the drone's own mass gives 1.63 kg, and forgetting both gives 3.26 kg.

aero-w3-q15.question: A 50 m³ helium weather balloon is at sea level (ρ_air = 1.225, ρ_He = 0.169 kg/m³). The envelope and instruments have a mass of 20 kg. Taking g = 9.81 m/s², what is the net upward force just after release?
aero-w3-q15.explanation: Net lift of the gas = 50 × (1.225 − 0.169) = 52.8 kg. Subtract the payload: 52.8 − 20 = 32.8 kg. Force = 32.8 × 9.81 ≈ 322 N. Trap: forgetting to subtract the 20 kg gives 518 N, not multiplying by g gives 32.8 (that is kg, not N), and forgetting to subtract the helium's weight gives 405 N.

aero-w4-q1.question: Wing flutter is a vibration that grows when air forces combine with the wing's elasticity. Which two fields are mainly needed together to understand it?
aero-w4-q1.explanation: In flutter, aerodynamic forces bend the wing and the bending changes the forces; this is an interaction of aerodynamics and structures (elasticity), called aeroelasticity. Trap: linking every vibration to the engine and picking propulsion.

aero-w4-q2.question: Which of these tasks belongs to the ground support field?
options: Choosing an airfoil for the wing
Designing the cooling of turbine blades
aero-w4-q2.explanation: Ground support covers everything that helps operate the vehicle from the ground: maintenance, refuelling, air traffic control, airports, launch sites and mission control. Choosing an airfoil is aerodynamics, a control law is flight dynamics and control, and turbine cooling is propulsion.

aero-w4-q3.question: A light aircraft has a mass of 1,100 kg and a wing area of 16.2 m² (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is its wing loading?
aero-w4-q3.explanation: W = 1,100 × 9.81 = 10,791 N. W/S = 10,791/16.2 ≈ 666 N/m². Trap: 67.9 is really in kg/m² (g was forgotten) but is labelled N/m²; 1.50 × 10⁻³ is the inverse ratio S/W, and 174,800 comes from multiplying weight by area.

aero-w4-q4.question: A twin-engine airliner has 120 kN of thrust per engine and a take-off mass of 75,000 kg (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is its thrust-to-weight ratio at take-off?
aero-w4-q4.explanation: Total thrust = 2 × 120 = 240 kN. Weight = 75,000 × 9.81 = 735,750 N. T/W = 240,000/735,750 ≈ 0.33. Trap: using only one engine gives 0.16, forgetting g gives 3.2 (newtons divided by kg), and taking the ratio upside down gives 3.07.

aero-w4-q5.question: An aircraft has a fixed MTOW of 80,000 kg. Operating empty weight is 44,000 kg and mission fuel is 20,000 kg. New, more reliable avionics add 1,500 kg to the empty weight, with fuel unchanged. What is the maximum payload now?
aero-w4-q5.explanation: Before, payload = 80,000 − 44,000 − 20,000 = 16,000 kg. With an empty weight of 45,500 kg, payload = 80,000 − 45,500 − 20,000 = 14,500 kg. With MTOW fixed, every extra kg of structure or avionics comes straight out of payload. Trap: 17,500 kg comes from adding the 1,500 instead of subtracting it, and 36,000 kg from forgetting the fuel.

aero-w4-q6.question: Stall speed V_s = √(2W/(ρ S C_Lmax)). Keeping weight and C_Lmax the same, a designer increases wing area by 25%. How does the stall speed change?
aero-w4-q6.explanation: V_s ∝ 1/√S. New S = 1.25 S, so new V_s = V_s/√1.25 = 0.894 V_s, i.e. about 10.6% lower. Trap: forgetting the square root and using 1/1.25 = 0.8 (20% lower), or simply assuming 25% lower. The gain (lower stall speed) comes with the cost of a heavier wing and more drag.

aero-w4-q7.question: Designing autopilot control laws and checking whether the aircraft stays stable after a disturbance is the job of which discipline?
aero-w4-q7.explanation: How the vehicle moves under forces and moments, whether it is stable, and how to control it with control laws is flight dynamics and control. Trap: propulsion is about thrust, structures about carrying loads, and ground support about maintenance or ATC.

aero-w4-q8.question: Which field do navigation receivers, cockpit displays, flight computers and radios belong to?
aero-w4-q8.explanation: On-board electronics, that is navigation, sensors, displays, flight computers, radios and data links, is the avionics and communication field. Trap: aerodynamics covers air forces, propulsion covers thrust, and structures covers airframe loads.

aero-w4-q9.question: Which kind of aircraft usually has a thrust-to-weight ratio (T/W) of about 1 or more?
aero-w4-q9.explanation: Fighters have T/W of about 1 or more, while airliners are about 0.25–0.4. Trap: an airliner and a cargo turboprop have T/W well below 1, and a glider has no engine at all.

aero-w4-q10.question: A four-engine transport aircraft has a take-off mass of 90,000 kg and each engine gives 60 kN of thrust (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is T/W at take-off?
aero-w4-q10.explanation: Total thrust = 4 × 60 = 240 kN. Weight = 90,000 × 9.81 = 882,900 N. T/W = 240,000/882,900 ≈ 0.27. Trap: taking only one engine gives 0.068, two engines gives 0.14, and not multiplying by g (dividing by the mass) gives 2.67.

aero-w4-q11.question: All the motors of a 3 kg VTOL drone together can give 25 N of thrust (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is its T/W, and can it hover vertically?
aero-w4-q11.explanation: Weight = 3 × 9.81 = 29.43 N. T/W = 25/29.43 ≈ 0.85. Vertical hover needs thrust ≥ weight, that is T/W ≥ 1, so it cannot hover. Trap: forgetting g gives 8.3, taking the ratio the other way (W/T) gives 1.18, and taking mass/thrust gives 0.12.

aero-w4-q12.question: A 2-seat aircraft has an MTOW of 1,200 kg and an operating empty weight of 750 kg. The pilot and passenger together weigh 240 kg. The engine burns 30 kg/h of fuel and a 45 min reserve is required. At MTOW, what is the longest flight that can be planned (not counting the reserve)?
aero-w4-q12.explanation: Fuel = 1,200 − 750 − 240 = 210 kg. Reserve = 0.75 × 30 = 22.5 kg. Usable = 187.5 kg, time = 187.5/30 = 6.25 h. Trap: forgetting the reserve gives 7.0 h, taking 45 min as 0.45 h gives 6.55 h, and forgetting the people's weight gives 15 h.

aero-w4-q13.question: A trainer has a mass of 1,200 kg and a wing area of 15 m². The designer increases the wing area to 18 m², which makes the wing structure 30 kg heavier (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is the new wing loading?
aero-w4-q13.explanation: New mass = 1,230 kg, W = 1,230 × 9.81 = 12,066 N. W/S = 12,066/18 ≈ 670 N/m². Trap: forgetting the extra 30 kg gives 654 N/m², using the old 15 m² area gives 804 N/m², and forgetting g gives 68.3 (which is really kg/m²).

aero-w4-q14.question: A twin-engine fighter has a mass of 12,000 kg and the designer wants T/W = 1.1 (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is the minimum thrust each engine must give?
aero-w4-q14.explanation: Weight = 12,000 × 9.81 = 117,720 N. Total thrust = 1.1 × 117,720 ≈ 129,500 N. Each engine = 129,500/2 ≈ 64.7 kN. Trap: 129.5 kN is the total for both engines, forgetting g gives 6.6 kN, and taking T/W = 1 gives 58.9 kN.

aero-w4-q15.question: An aircraft takes off with a mass of 80,000 kg and its 2 engines together give 220 kN of thrust (g = 9.81 m/s²). By the end of the mission 20,000 kg of fuel has been burned and thrust is unchanged. What is T/W now?
aero-w4-q15.explanation: New mass = 80,000 − 20,000 = 60,000 kg, W = 588,600 N. T/W = 220,000/588,600 ≈ 0.37 (it was 0.28 at take-off). Burning fuel lowers the weight and raises T/W. Trap: 0.28 is the take-off value, using one engine (110 kN) gives 0.19, and forgetting g gives 3.67.

aero-w5-q1.question: What is the 'chord' of an airfoil?
options: The mean curved line between the upper and lower surfaces
The straight line joining the leading edge and the trailing edge
The distance from one wingtip to the other
The maximum thickness of the airfoil
aero-w5-q1.explanation: The chord is the straight line from the leading edge to the trailing edge, and the angle of attack is measured from this line. Trap: the mean curved line is the camber line, and the wingtip-to-wingtip distance is the wingspan.

aero-w5-q2.question: If the airspeed is doubled while density, wing area and C_L stay the same, what happens to lift?
aero-w5-q2.explanation: In L = ½ρV²SC_L, lift is proportional to V². Doubling V ⇒ V² becomes four times ⇒ lift becomes 4 times. Trap: treating lift as proportional to V and saying 2 times.

aero-w5-q3.question: At sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) a wing flies at 50 m/s. Wing area is 16 m² and C_L = 0.6. What is the lift?
aero-w5-q3.explanation: q = ½ × 1.225 × 50² = 1,531.25 Pa. L = q S C_L = 1,531.25 × 16 × 0.6 = 14,700 N. Trap: forgetting the ½ gives 29,400 N, not squaring V gives 294 N, and forgetting C_L gives 24,500 N.

aero-w5-q4.question: An airliner flies at 11 km at 250 m/s (true airspeed), where the speed of sound is 295 m/s. What is its Mach number?
aero-w5-q4.explanation: M = V/a = 250/295 ≈ 0.847, i.e. high subsonic, at the edge of transonic. Trap: using the sea-level speed of sound of 340 m/s gives 0.735; 1.18 and 1.36 come from taking the ratio upside down.

aero-w5-q5.question: A wing has a chord of 1.2 m and flies at 40 m/s at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, μ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s). What is the Reynolds number based on chord?
aero-w5-q5.explanation: Re = ρVc/μ = (1.225 × 40 × 1.2)/(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 58.8/(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) ≈ 3.27 × 10⁶. Trap: forgetting ρ gives 2.67 × 10⁶, and taking the ratio upside down (μ/ρVc) gives 3.06 × 10⁻⁷, which is dimensionless but is not Re.

aero-w5-q6.question: An aircraft has a mass of 1,000 kg, a wing area of 15 m² and C_Lmax = 1.5. What is its level-flight stall speed at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
aero-w5-q6.explanation: W = 9,810 N. V_s = √(2W/(ρ S C_Lmax)) = √(19,620/(1.225 × 15 × 1.5)) = √(19,620/27.5625) = √711.8 ≈ 26.7 m/s. Trap: dropping the 2 in the formula gives 18.9 m/s, forgetting the square root gives 712, and forgetting g (treating mass as weight) gives 8.52 m/s.

aero-w5-q7.question: The angle of attack (α) is the angle between which two things?
options: The nose direction and the ground
The camber line and the trailing edge
The chord line and the relative wind
aero-w5-q7.explanation: α is the angle between the chord line and the oncoming air (relative wind). Trap: the angle of the nose to the ground is the pitch angle, not α; in a climb the pitch can be large while α is small.

aero-w5-q8.question: Which drag, produced by wingtip vortices while making lift, is larger at low speed?
aero-w5-q8.explanation: Making lift creates wingtip vortices and hence induced drag, which is larger at low speed (high C_L). Trap: skin friction is surface rubbing, wave drag comes from shock waves at high speed, and form drag from flow separation.

aero-w5-q9.question: An aircraft is flying at M = 1.5. Which speed regime is this?
aero-w5-q9.explanation: Regimes: subsonic M < 0.8, transonic about 0.8–1.2, supersonic 1.2–5, hypersonic M > 5. M = 1.5 is supersonic. Trap: being above 1 does not make it hypersonic; hypersonic starts above 5.

aero-w5-q10.question: At sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) an aircraft is flying at 60 m/s. The wing area is 16 m² and C_D = 0.03. What is the drag?
aero-w5-q10.explanation: q = ½ × 1.225 × 60² = 2,205 Pa. D = q S C_D = 2,205 × 16 × 0.03 ≈ 1,058 N. Trap: forgetting the ½ gives 2,117 N, not squaring V gives 17.6 N, and forgetting to multiply by C_D gives 35,280 N.

aero-w5-q11.question: An airliner weighs 600 kN and has L/D = 18 in steady level cruise. What total thrust must the engines give?
aero-w5-q11.explanation: In level flight L = W = 600 kN and thrust = drag. D = L/(L/D) = 600/18 ≈ 33.3 kN. Trap: setting thrust equal to weight gives 600 kN, multiplying by L/D gives 10,800 kN, and writing L/D itself in kN gives 18 kN.

aero-w5-q12.question: A jet is flying at M = 0.80 at 11 km (speed of sound 295 m/s). If it keeps the same true airspeed at sea level (speed of sound 340 m/s), what will its Mach number be there?
aero-w5-q12.explanation: TAS = 0.80 × 295 = 236 m/s. At sea level M = 236/340 ≈ 0.694. The speed of sound is higher lower down, so the same speed gives a lower Mach. Trap: treating Mach as fixed like a speed gives 0.80, inverting the ratio (340/295) gives 0.922, and squaring the ratio gives 0.602.

aero-w5-q13.question: An aircraft has a mass of 1,200 kg and a wing area of 16 m². What C_L is needed for level flight at 60 m/s at 3 km (ρ = 0.909 kg/m³)? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
aero-w5-q13.explanation: L = W = 1,200 × 9.81 = 11,772 N. q = ½ × 0.909 × 60² = 1,636 Pa. C_L = 11,772/(1,636 × 16) ≈ 0.45. Thinner air needs a higher C_L at the same speed. Trap: using sea-level density gives 0.33, forgetting the ½ gives 0.22, and treating mass as weight gives 0.046.

aero-w5-q14.question: An aircraft has a mass of 1,000 kg, a wing area of 15 m² and C_Lmax = 1.5 with flaps up, which gives a sea-level stall speed of 26.7 m/s. With flaps down C_Lmax becomes 2.1. What is the new stall speed?
aero-w5-q14.explanation: V_s ∝ 1/√C_Lmax, so V_s = 26.7 × √(1.5/2.1) = 26.7 × 0.845 ≈ 22.6 m/s. Trap: forgetting the square root and using the plain ratio gives 19.1 m/s, inverting the ratio gives 31.6 m/s, and assuming flaps do not change stall speed gives 26.7 m/s.

aero-w5-q15.question: A small drone (chord 0.2 m) flies at 15 m/s and a light aircraft (chord 1.5 m) at 60 m/s, both at sea level. How many times the drone's chord-based Reynolds number is the aircraft's?
aero-w5-q15.explanation: Re = ρVL/μ; ρ and μ are the same, so the ratio = (60 × 1.5)/(15 × 0.2) = 90/3 = 30. This is why a drone behaves differently aerodynamically. Trap: using only the speed ratio gives 4, only the chord ratio gives 7.5, and squaring the ratio gives 900.

aero-w6-q1.question: The pilot moves the control stick to the left. Which control surface acts, and about which axis does the aircraft rotate?
aero-w6-q1.explanation: Moving the stick left or right works the ailerons: one goes up and the other down, so one wing gains lift and the other loses it, and the aircraft rolls about the longitudinal axis. Trap: seeing the aircraft turn and thinking of yaw or the rudder; a turn starts with roll (bank).

aero-w6-q2.question: About which axis does pitch motion (nose up and down) take place?
aero-w6-q2.explanation: When the nose moves up and down, the wingtip-to-wingtip line stays in place, so pitch is about the lateral axis. Trap: hearing 'nose' and choosing the longitudinal axis; rotation about the longitudinal axis is roll.

aero-w6-q3.question: An aircraft's neutral point is at 0.42 c̄ of the mean chord and its CG is at 0.28 c̄ (both from the leading edge). What are the static margin and the stability?
aero-w6-q3.explanation: SM = (x_NP − x_CG)/c̄ = 0.42 − 0.28 = 0.14 = 14%. The CG is ahead of the neutral point, so the aircraft is statically stable. Trap: subtracting the wrong way round to get −14%, or using a ratio like 0.28/0.42 = 0.67, which is not the definition of static margin.

aero-w6-q4.question: In an aircraft the wing lift is 12,000 N and acts 0.15 m behind the CG. The horizontal tail is 5 m behind the CG. Ignore other moments. What force must the tail give for trim?
aero-w6-q4.explanation: The wing's nose-down moment = 12,000 × 0.15 = 1,800 N·m. To cancel it the tail must give a nose-up moment; the tail is behind the CG, so its force must act downward: F = 1,800/5 = 360 N downward. Trap: 1,800 is a moment (N·m), not a force; and an upward tail force would add to the nose-down moment.

aero-w6-q5.question: If an aircraft's vertical tail is made much smaller, which stability is most directly affected?
options: No stability changes, only drag falls
Lateral (roll) stability, which comes from dihedral
aero-w6-q5.explanation: The vertical tail works like a weathercock: in a sideslip it gets a side force that turns the nose back into the relative wind. So a smaller vertical tail reduces directional (yaw) stability. Trap: pitch stability comes from the horizontal tail and CG position, and roll stability mainly from dihedral.

aero-w6-q6.question: An aircraft has a mean chord c̄ = 2 m, its neutral point is at 0.40 c̄ and its CG starts at 0.25 c̄. During flight, fuel burn moves the CG 0.36 m aft. What are the static margin and stability now?
aero-w6-q6.explanation: CG shift = 0.36/2 = 0.18 c̄, so the new CG = 0.25 + 0.18 = 0.43 c̄. SM = 0.40 − 0.43 = −0.03 = −3%, so the CG is now behind the neutral point and the aircraft is statically unstable. Trap: adding the 0.36 m directly without dividing by the chord gives −21%, and ignoring the shift gives +15%.

aero-w6-q7.question: Which motion does the rudder control, and about which axis does that motion happen?
aero-w6-q7.explanation: The rudder is on the vertical tail and gives yaw, which happens about the vertical (normal) axis. Trap: roll comes from the ailerons and pitch from the elevator; yaw is not about the lateral axis.

aero-w6-q8.question: What is the job of the spoilers that rise from the top of the wing after landing?
options: To raise C_Lmax and lower stall speed
To remove the pilot's stick force
To reduce lift and increase drag
aero-w6-q8.explanation: Spoilers reduce lift and increase drag, which puts the aircraft's weight on the wheels so the brakes work well. Trap: raising C_Lmax is what flaps do, removing stick force is what trim tabs do, and directional stability comes from the vertical tail.

aero-w6-q9.question: Wing dihedral (wingtips slightly raised) mainly helps which kind of stability?
aero-w6-q9.explanation: Dihedral helps bring the wings level after a roll disturbance, that is lateral stability. Trap: pitch stability comes from the positions of the CG and neutral point, and yaw stability from the vertical tail.

aero-w6-q10.question: An aircraft has mean chord c̄ = 1.5 m. The neutral point is at 0.45 c̄ and the CG is 0.48 m behind the leading edge. What is the static margin?
aero-w6-q10.explanation: CG = 0.48/1.5 = 0.32 c̄. SM = (0.45 − 0.32) = 0.13 = 13%, positive, so stable. Trap: taking 0.48 m directly as 0.48 c̄ gives −3%, the CG position itself (32%) is not the SM, and writing the difference in metres (0.195 m) as a percentage gives 19.5%.

aero-w6-q11.question: After a gust an aircraft heads back towards its original attitude, but it oscillates and each oscillation is larger than the last. How would you classify it?
aero-w6-q11.explanation: Its first tendency is to return, so it is statically stable. But the oscillations grow instead of dying out, so it is dynamically unstable. Trap: a tendency to return does not guarantee dynamic stability; growing oscillation is dynamic instability.

aero-w6-q12.question: An aircraft weighs 10,000 N. The wing lift acts 0.2 m behind the CG and the horizontal tail is 5 m behind the CG. Ignore other moments. What tail force is needed for trim, and in which direction?
aero-w6-q12.explanation: Moments: 0.2 L_w = 5 F_t ⇒ F_t = 0.04 L_w. Vertical: L_w = 10,000 + F_t ⇒ 0.96 L_w = 10,000 ⇒ L_w ≈ 10,417 N, F_t ≈ 417 N down. Trap: using the weight instead of L_w gives 400 N, taking the direction the wrong way gives upward, and not dividing by 5 m gives 2,000 N.

aero-w6-q13.question: An aircraft has c̄ = 2 m, the neutral point at 0.40 c̄ and the CG at 0.25 c̄. A safety rule requires a static margin of at least 5%. How many metres aft can cargo loading move the CG at most?
aero-w6-q13.explanation: Most aft allowed CG = 0.40 − 0.05 = 0.35 c̄. Shift = 0.35 − 0.25 = 0.10 c̄ = 0.10 × 2 = 0.20 m. Trap: going right up to the NP gives 0.30 m (SM would then be zero), writing the fraction as metres gives 0.10 m, and adding the 5% instead of subtracting it gives 0.40 m.

aero-w6-q14.question: In an 8,000 N aircraft, a forward CG shift means the wing lift now acts 0.2 m behind the CG (it was 0.1 m). The tail is 4 m behind the CG. Ignore other moments. What downward tail force is now needed for trim?
aero-w6-q14.explanation: Moments: 0.2 L_w = 4 F_t ⇒ F_t = 0.05 L_w. Vertical: L_w = 8,000 + 0.05 L_w ⇒ L_w ≈ 8,421 N, F_t ≈ 421 N. A forward CG makes the tail push down harder, so trim drag rises. Trap: doubling the old 205 N gives 410 N, using the weight instead of L_w gives 400 N, and 205 N is the old value.

aero-w6-q15.question: An aircraft has c̄ = 2.5 m and its static margin is now −4%. To make the static margin 10%, how far and in which direction must the CG be moved?
aero-w6-q15.explanation: SM must go from −0.04 to +0.10, a change of 0.14 c̄. 0.14 × 2.5 = 0.35 m. Raising the SM means moving the CG further ahead of the NP. Trap: the opposite direction gives aft, taking a difference of only 6% (10 − 4) gives 0.15 m, and writing the fraction as metres gives 0.14 m.

aero-w7-q1.question: Which pressure does an aircraft's pressure altimeter use to show altitude?
aero-w7-q1.explanation: The altimeter takes the outside static pressure from the static port and converts it to altitude using the standard-atmosphere relation. Trap: total and dynamic pressure depend on speed, so they are used by the ASI; cabin pressure is inside the aircraft and does not tell the outside altitude.

aero-w7-q2.question: What do the gyroscopes in an IMU measure directly?
options: Angular rate (how fast it is rotating)
aero-w7-q2.explanation: Gyroscopes measure angular rate (rad/s or deg/s); integrating it gives attitude. Linear acceleration is measured by accelerometers, and magnetic heading comes from a magnetometer or compass. Trap: swapping the jobs of the accelerometer and the gyro.

aero-w7-q3.question: At sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) the difference between pitot and static pressure is 2,450 Pa. What is the airspeed?
aero-w7-q3.explanation: V = √(2Δp/ρ) = √(2 × 2,450/1.225) = √4,000 ≈ 63.2 m/s. Trap: forgetting the 2 gives √2,000 = 44.7 m/s, forgetting the square root gives 4,000, and using 4 instead of 2 gives 89.4 m/s.

aero-w7-q4.question: An aircraft's equivalent airspeed (EAS) is 80 m/s at an altitude where ρ = 0.736 kg/m³ (ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³). What is the true airspeed?
aero-w7-q4.explanation: TAS = EAS × √(ρ₀/ρ) = 80 × √(1.225/0.736) = 80 × 1.290 ≈ 103 m/s. In thinner air a higher true speed is needed for the same dynamic pressure. Trap: taking the ratio upside down gives 62.0 m/s, and forgetting the square root gives 133 m/s.

aero-w7-q5.question: During a climb the static port is completely blocked by ice (the pitot tube is fine). What will the altimeter show?
options: It keeps showing the correct altitude
It stays stuck at the altitude where the blockage happened
It shows a rise much faster than the real altitude
aero-w7-q5.explanation: The altimeter works only on static pressure. Once the port is blocked, the pressure inside stays at its value at the moment of blockage, so the altimeter sticks at that altitude and the VSI shows zero. Trap: thinking that no pressure means a zero reading; the trapped air keeps its pressure.

aero-w7-q6.question: Near sea level a drone's barometric sensor sees the static pressure drop from 101,325 Pa to 100,123 Pa. Taking ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s² (Δp = ρgΔh), how far did the drone climb?
aero-w7-q6.explanation: Δp = 101,325 − 100,123 = 1,202 Pa. Δh = Δp/(ρg) = 1,202/(1.225 × 9.81) = 1,202/12.02 ≈ 100 m. Trap: forgetting g gives 981 m, multiplying by ρg gives about 14,400, and treating 1 Pa as 1 m gives 1,202 m.

aero-w7-q7.question: Which instrument uses both the pitot (total) and static pressures?
aero-w7-q7.explanation: The ASI gets speed from p₀ − p, the dynamic pressure, so it needs both. Trap: the altimeter and VSI use only static pressure, and the compass does not use pressure at all.

aero-w7-q8.question: What is the minimum number of satellites a GPS receiver needs to find its 3D position and its own clock error?
aero-w7-q8.explanation: Three position unknowns (x, y, z) plus the receiver clock error make 4 unknowns, so at least 4 satellites. Trap: 3 satellites would be enough only if the receiver clock were perfect.

aero-w7-q9.question: Why is a heater fitted to an aircraft's pitot tube?
options: To raise the static port pressure
To make the GPS signal stronger
To keep ice from blocking the pitot tube
To measure the outside air density
aero-w7-q9.explanation: If ice blocks the pitot tube the ASI shows a wrong speed, so pitot heaters are fitted. Trap: the heater does not raise static pressure, has nothing to do with GPS, and does not measure density.

aero-w7-q10.question: An altimeter's reference pressure is set wrong by 1,000 Pa (10 hPa). Near sea level, taking ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s² (Δp = ρgΔh), by about how much will the indicated altitude be wrong?
aero-w7-q10.explanation: Δh = Δp/(ρg) = 1,000/(1.225 × 9.81) = 1,000/12.02 ≈ 83 m. Trap: using 100 Pa gives 8.3 m, a misplaced decimal gives 833 m, and 12 is the pressure drop per metre (Pa/m), not the altitude error.

aero-w7-q11.question: Both the pitot tube and its drain hole are blocked by ice (the static port is fine). The aircraft climbs at constant true speed. What will the ASI show?
aero-w7-q11.explanation: The pressure in the pitot is trapped, while static pressure falls in a climb. So p₀ − p rises and the ASI behaves like an altimeter, showing increasing speed. Trap: decreasing speed shows in a descent, and a blocked static port freezes the altimeter rather than zeroing the ASI.

aero-w7-q12.question: An aircraft flies at a true airspeed of 90 m/s at an altitude where ρ = 0.909 kg/m³. The ASI is calibrated at ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³. Ignoring errors and compressibility, what will the ASI read (EAS)?
aero-w7-q12.explanation: EAS = TAS × √(ρ/ρ₀) = 90 × √(0.909/1.225) = 90 × 0.861 ≈ 77.5 m/s. At altitude the ASI reads below the true speed. Trap: inverting the ratio (the TAS formula) gives 104.5 m/s, taking the ASI as TAS gives 90.0 m/s, and forgetting the square root gives 66.8 m/s.

aero-w7-q13.question: An aircraft at 3 km (ρ = 0.909 kg/m³, ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³) flies at an EAS of 70 m/s into a 15 m/s headwind. Ignoring errors, what is its ground speed?
aero-w7-q13.explanation: TAS = 70 × √(1.225/0.909) = 70 × 1.161 ≈ 81.3 m/s. Subtract the headwind: 81.3 − 15 ≈ 66.3 m/s. Trap: subtracting the wind from the EAS gives 55.0 m/s, adding the headwind gives 96.3 m/s, and adding the wind to the EAS gives 85.0 m/s.

aero-w7-q14.question: Near sea level a drone's barometer sees the static pressure fall by 1,800 Pa in 30 s. Taking ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s² (Δp = ρgΔh), what is the average climb rate?
aero-w7-q14.explanation: Δh = 1,800/(1.225 × 9.81) ≈ 150 m. Rate = 150/30 ≈ 5.0 m/s. Trap: dividing the pressure drop directly by 30 gives 60 (that is Pa/s), writing the height as the rate gives 150 m/s, and a misplaced decimal gives 0.5 m/s.

aero-w7-q15.question: Near sea level an aircraft's pitot-static system has p₀ − p = 3,000 Pa (ASI ≈ 70 m/s). Then the pitot tube and drain hole are both blocked, and the aircraft descends 150 m at the same true speed. Taking ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s², what will the ASI now show?
aero-w7-q15.explanation: The trapped p₀ stays the same, but 150 m lower the static pressure rises by ρgΔh = 1.225 × 9.81 × 150 ≈ 1,802 Pa. New Δp = 3,000 − 1,802 ≈ 1,198 Pa, V = √(2 × 1,198/1.225) ≈ 44.2 m/s. Trap: assuming the blockage has no effect gives 70.0 m/s, and adding the pressure instead of subtracting gives 88.5 m/s, and forgetting the 2 in V = √(2Δp/ρ) gives 31.3 m/s.

aero-w8-q1.question: Which engine cannot give thrust to an aircraft standing on the runway (zero forward speed)?
aero-w8-q1.explanation: A ramjet has no compressor; it needs high forward speed of the vehicle to compress the air. At zero speed there is no compression and so no thrust. Trap: treating the rocket as air-breathing too; a rocket carries its own oxidiser and gives thrust even at zero speed.

aero-w8-q2.question: Why does a rocket engine work even in space (vacuum)?
options: There is no drag in space, so no thrust is needed
It carries its own oxidiser along with the fuel
It takes oxygen in through an intake
aero-w8-q2.explanation: Combustion needs both fuel and oxidiser. A rocket carries both, so it needs no outside air and makes thrust in vacuum by throwing gas backwards. Trap: no drag does not mean no thrust is needed; thrust is needed to change speed (Δv).

aero-w8-q3.question: A turbojet flies at 220 m/s. Air mass flow is 80 kg/s and exhaust velocity is 520 m/s. The nozzle is fully expanded and fuel mass is ignored. What is the net thrust?
aero-w8-q3.explanation: F = ṁ(V_e − V₀) = 80 × (520 − 220) = 80 × 300 = 24,000 N = 24.0 kN. Trap: forgetting the momentum of the incoming air and taking ṁV_e = 41.6 kN, or adding the velocities to get 59.2 kN.

aero-w8-q4.question: A total of 600 kg/s of air passes through a turbofan with a bypass ratio of 9. How much air goes through the core (the part with the combustor)?
aero-w8-q4.explanation: BPR = bypass/core = 9, so total = core + 9 × core = 10 × core. Core = 600/10 = 60 kg/s and bypass = 540 kg/s. Trap: dividing the total straight by 9 to get 66.7 kg/s, or taking the bypass flow (540) as the core.

aero-w8-q5.question: A rocket engine gives 750 kN of thrust in vacuum and burns 250 kg/s of propellant. Taking g₀ = 9.81 m/s², what is its specific impulse?
aero-w8-q5.explanation: I_sp = F/(ṁg₀) = 750,000/(250 × 9.81) = 750,000/2,452.5 ≈ 306 s. The effective exhaust velocity is 3,000 m/s. Trap: 3,000 is a velocity (m/s), not seconds; not converting kN to N gives 0.306, and multiplying by g₀ instead of dividing gives 29,430.

aero-w8-q6.question: A rocket stage has an initial mass of 50,000 kg and a burnout mass of 12,500 kg. The engine has I_sp = 300 s and g₀ = 9.81 m/s². What ideal Δv does the Tsiolkovsky equation give?
aero-w8-q6.explanation: Mass ratio = 50,000/12,500 = 4. Δv = I_sp g₀ ln 4 = 300 × 9.81 × 1.386 ≈ 4,080 m/s = 4.08 km/s. Trap: multiplying by the mass ratio instead of taking ln gives 11.77 km/s, using log₁₀ gives 1.77 km/s, and forgetting g₀ gives 0.416 km/s.

aero-w8-q7.question: How is a turbofan's bypass ratio (BPR) defined?
options: Core mass flow / bypass mass flow
Bypass mass flow / core mass flow
aero-w8-q7.explanation: BPR = bypass mass flow / core mass flow. For example BPR 9 means 9 kg/s goes around for every 1 kg/s through the core. Trap: the inverse ratio is not the BPR, and a ratio of speeds is not called the bypass ratio.

aero-w8-q8.question: A regional aircraft must fly short routes at about M 0.5 as fuel-efficiently as possible. Which engine fits best?
aero-w8-q8.explanation: At low speed (up to about M 0.6–0.7) a propeller speeds up a lot of air by a little, so a turboprop is the most efficient. Trap: an afterburning turbojet is for supersonic flight, a ramjet for M 2–5, and a rocket for space.

aero-w8-q9.question: What is special about a scramjet?
options: It gives thrust at zero speed
aero-w8-q9.explanation: A scramjet has no compressor and burns fuel in supersonic flow, so it is meant for hypersonic speeds. Trap: ramjets and scramjets give no thrust at zero speed, and carrying an oxidiser is a feature of rockets.

aero-w8-q10.question: An aircraft flies at 200 m/s and its engine exhaust velocity is 300 m/s. What is the propulsive efficiency η_p = 2/(1 + V_e/V₀)?
aero-w8-q10.explanation: V_e/V₀ = 300/200 = 1.5. η_p = 2/(1 + 1.5) = 2/2.5 = 0.80. Trap: just taking V₀/V_e gives 0.67, forgetting the 2 gives 0.40, and inverting the fraction gives 1.25, which is impossible since it is above 1.

aero-w8-q11.question: A rocket engine has I_sp = 280 s and burns 150 kg/s of propellant. Taking g₀ = 9.81 m/s², what is its thrust? (F = I_sp g₀ ṁ)
aero-w8-q11.explanation: F = 280 × 9.81 × 150 = 412,020 N ≈ 412 kN. Trap: forgetting g₀ gives 42.0 kN, a slip converting N to kN gives 4,120 kN, and dividing by ṁ instead of multiplying gives 18.3.

aero-w8-q12.question: At sea level (p_a = 101.325 kPa) a rocket has ṁ = 200 kg/s, V_e = 2,800 m/s, nozzle exit pressure p_e = 70 kPa and exit area A_e = 1.2 m². What is the thrust F = ṁV_e + (p_e − p_a)A_e?
aero-w8-q12.explanation: ṁV_e = 200 × 2,800 = 560,000 N. Pressure term = (70,000 − 101,325) × 1.2 = −37,590 N. F = 560,000 − 37,590 ≈ 522 kN. The nozzle is over-expanded, so the pressure term reduces thrust. Trap: ignoring the pressure term gives 560 kN, flipping its sign gives 598 kN, and taking only the size of the pressure term gives 37.6 kN.

aero-w8-q13.question: A turbofan flies at 230 m/s. 50 kg/s of air leaves the core at 500 m/s and 300 kg/s leaves the bypass at 300 m/s. The nozzles are fully expanded and fuel mass is ignored. What is the total net thrust?
aero-w8-q13.explanation: Core: 50 × (500 − 230) = 13,500 N. Bypass: 300 × (300 − 230) = 21,000 N. Total = 34,500 N = 34.5 kN (here BPR = 6, and most of the thrust comes from the bypass). Trap: counting only the core gives 13.5 kN, only the bypass gives 21.0 kN, and forgetting the incoming air momentum (V₀) gives 115 kN.

aero-w8-q14.question: An upper stage has an initial mass of 20,000 kg and needs an ideal Δv of 3 km/s. The engine has I_sp = 320 s and g₀ = 9.81 m/s². How much propellant is needed? (Δv = I_sp g₀ ln(m₀/m_f))
aero-w8-q14.explanation: ln(m₀/m_f) = 3,000/(320 × 9.81) = 0.9556, so m₀/m_f = e^0.9556 ≈ 2.600. m_f = 20,000/2.600 ≈ 7,690 kg, propellant = 20,000 − 7,690 ≈ 12,300 kg. Trap: 7,690 kg is the burnout mass, not the propellant; using log₁₀ instead of ln gives 17,800 kg, and treating ln as linear (20,000 × 0.9556) gives 19,100 kg.

aero-w8-q15.question: A 2-stage rocket has a lift-off mass of 100 t. After stage 1 burns, the mass is 40 t; then the 10 t empty stage is dropped. Stage 2 starts at 30 t and burns out at 12 t. Both stages have I_sp = 300 s, g₀ = 9.81 m/s². What is the total ideal Δv?
aero-w8-q15.explanation: Stage 1: 2,943 × ln(100/40) = 2,943 × 0.916 ≈ 2.70 km/s. Stage 2: 2,943 × ln(30/12) ≈ 2.70 km/s. Total ≈ 5.39 km/s. Without dropping the empty stage (all propellant together, 100 → 22 t) you would get only ln(100/22) × 2,943 ≈ 4.46 km/s; that is why rockets stage. Trap: 2.70 km/s is just one stage, and using log₁₀ gives 2.34 km/s.

aero-w9-q1.question: What is the main job of ribs in a wing structure?
options: Carrying the main bending load along the span
Keeping the airfoil shape and passing skin loads to the spars
aero-w9-q1.explanation: Ribs are chord-wise frames that keep the airfoil shape, support the skin and stringers and transfer their loads to the spars. Trap: the main bending load is carried by the spar, not the rib; landing shocks are taken by the landing gear's shock absorber.

aero-w9-q2.question: In a semi-monocoque fuselage, what carries the load?
options: The skin together with frames and stringers
aero-w9-q2.explanation: In a semi-monocoque the thin skin does not carry load alone; frames and stringers support it and they all share the load. Trap: 'only the skin' is the definition of a pure monocoque.

aero-w9-q3.question: A 1,200 kg aircraft makes a level turn at 60° bank (g = 9.81 m/s²). How much lift must the wings produce?
aero-w9-q3.explanation: In a level turn n = 1/cos 60° = 2. W = 1,200 × 9.81 = 11,772 N, so L = nW = 23,544 N. Trap: taking n = 1 and writing just the weight (11,772 N); 13,593 N comes from using cos 30°, and 2,400 from forgetting g.

aero-w9-q4.question: A landing gear strut carries an axial load of 60 kN and has a cross-sectional area of 5 cm². What is the normal stress in the strut?
aero-w9-q4.explanation: A = 5 cm² = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m². σ = F/A = 60,000/(5 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.2 × 10⁸ Pa = 120 MPa. Trap: converting cm² with 10⁻³ or 10⁻⁵ gives 12 or 1,200 MPa, and not changing kN to N gives 0.12 MPa.

aero-w9-q5.question: An aircraft has a positive limit load factor of 3.8 and a factor of safety of 1.5. For what ultimate load factor must the structure be designed?
aero-w9-q5.explanation: Ultimate = limit × factor of safety = 3.8 × 1.5 = 5.7. Trap: dividing 3.8 by 1.5 gives 2.53, and adding them gives 5.3; the factor of safety multiplies.

aero-w9-q6.question: A pressurised fuselage has a radius of 1.9 m and a skin thickness of 1.6 mm. The pressure difference between cabin and outside is 55 kPa. What is the hoop stress in the skin (σ = Δp·r/t)?
aero-w9-q6.explanation: σ = 55,000 × 1.9/0.0016 = 6.53 × 10⁷ Pa ≈ 65.3 MPa. Trap: 32.7 MPa is the longitudinal stress (Δp·r/(2t)); leaving the thickness in mm gives 0.0653 MPa, and using the diameter instead of the radius gives 130.6 MPa.

aero-w9-q7.question: What is the main job of the spars in a wing structure?
options: To keep the chord-wise airfoil shape
To stiffen the skin against buckling
To carry the bending load along the wing
To absorb the landing impact energy
aero-w9-q7.explanation: Spars are the main beams running along the wing and carry the bending load. Trap: ribs keep the airfoil shape, stringers protect the skin from buckling, and the oleo strut absorbs landing energy.

aero-w9-q8.question: Which landing gear layout is most common on aircraft today?
options: One central wheel plus wingtip wheels
aero-w9-q8.explanation: The tricycle layout is the most common today because it is stable on the ground and gives the pilot good visibility. Trap: tail-draggers are found on older and some light aircraft, and skids are seen on helicopters, not on typical aircraft.

aero-w9-q9.question: In steady level flight, what is the load factor n = L/W?
aero-w9-q9.explanation: In level flight lift = weight, so n = L/W = 1. Trap: 0 would mean no lift, 2 belongs to a level turn at 60° bank, and 9.81 is the value of g, not a load factor.

aero-w9-q10.question: An aircraft is in a level turn at 45° bank. What is the load factor?
aero-w9-q10.explanation: In a level turn n = 1/cos φ = 1/cos 45° = 1/0.707 ≈ 1.41. Trap: taking cos φ gives 0.71 (below 1, which is impossible), using the 30° value gives 1.15, and 2.00 is the value for 60° bank.

aero-w9-q11.question: A 2 m long aluminium rod (E = 72 GPa) carries a tensile stress of 144 MPa. Assuming the elastic region, by how much does the rod stretch?
aero-w9-q11.explanation: ε = σ/E = 144 × 10⁶/(72 × 10⁹) = 0.002. Stretch = 0.002 × 2,000 mm = 4 mm. Trap: a misplaced decimal gives 0.4 or 40 mm, and forgetting to multiply by the length gives just 2 (which is the strain × 1000).

aero-w9-q12.question: A pressurised fuselage has a radius of 2.0 m, a skin thickness of 2.0 mm and Δp = 60 kPa. What is the longitudinal stress Δp·r/(2t) in the skin?
aero-w9-q12.explanation: σ_long = 60,000 × 2.0/(2 × 0.002) = 120,000/0.004 = 3 × 10⁷ Pa = 30 MPa (the hoop stress is double, 60 MPa). Trap: 60 MPa is the hoop stress (or comes from using the diameter instead of the radius), 120 MPa from using the diameter in the hoop formula, and a wrong unit handling of t gives a tiny number like 0.03 MPa.

aero-w9-q13.question: One half-wing of an aircraft makes 25 kN of lift in level flight, acting effectively 3 m from the root. The limit load factor is 3.8 and the factor of safety is 1.5. What is the ultimate design bending moment at the root?
aero-w9-q13.explanation: Level: M = 25 × 3 = 75 kN·m. Limit: 75 × 3.8 = 285 kN·m. Ultimate: 285 × 1.5 ≈ 428 kN·m. Trap: 285 kN·m is only the limit moment (the 1.5 was forgotten), forgetting the load factor gives 113 kN·m, and 75 kN·m is just the level-flight moment.

aero-w9-q14.question: An aircraft has a positive limit load factor of 2.5. What is the maximum bank angle in a level turn without exceeding the limit load factor?
aero-w9-q14.explanation: n = 1/cos φ ⇒ cos φ = 1/2.5 = 0.4 ⇒ φ = cos⁻¹(0.4) ≈ 66.4°. Trap: taking sin⁻¹(0.4) gives 23.6°, taking tan⁻¹(2.5) gives 68.2°, and at 60.0° n is only 2, not the 2.5 limit.

aero-w9-q15.question: A landing gear strut has a limit axial load of 60 kN. The material's allowable stress is 300 MPa and a factor of safety of 1.5 must be applied for the ultimate load. What is the minimum cross-section area needed?
aero-w9-q15.explanation: Ultimate load = 60 × 1.5 = 90 kN. A = 90,000/(300 × 10⁶) = 3 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 3.0 cm² (1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²). Trap: forgetting the factor of safety gives 2.0 cm², dividing by 1.5 gives 1.33 cm², and a wrong m² to cm² conversion gives 0.30 cm².

aero-w10-q1.question: When a CFRP panel is joined directly with aluminium fasteners (in a humid environment), what is the biggest problem?
options: Galvanic corrosion: the aluminium corrodes quickly
No problem, both are light materials
aero-w10-q1.explanation: Carbon fibre and aluminium differ widely in electrochemical potential; in contact with moisture they form a galvanic cell and the aluminium (the anode) corrodes quickly. That is why titanium fasteners or insulation are used with CFRP. Trap: assuming that two light materials must also be compatible.

aero-w10-q2.question: In the context of materials, what is 'fatigue failure'?
options: Cracks growing under repeated (cyclic) loads, even at stresses below the static strength, until the part breaks
Breaking at once under a single very large load
The material melting at very high temperature
aero-w10-q2.explanation: In fatigue each load cycle grows the crack a little, and after thousands or millions of cycles the part can break even though the stress in each cycle is well below the static strength. Trap: breaking under a single overload is static failure, and rust is corrosion.

aero-w10-q3.question: Al alloy: σ = 500 MPa, ρ = 2,800 kg/m³. Ti alloy: σ = 900 MPa, ρ = 4,430 kg/m³. Based on specific strength (σ/ρ), which statement is correct?
options: Ti has higher strength, but Al's specific strength is about 2 times Ti's
aero-w10-q3.explanation: Al: 500 × 10⁶/2,800 ≈ 179 kN·m/kg. Ti: 900 × 10⁶/4,430 ≈ 203 kN·m/kg. Ti is slightly ahead, but against a 1.8 times gap in strength the specific strength differs by only about 14%, because Ti is also heavier. Trap: overestimating the effect of density and putting Al ahead.

aero-w10-q4.question: Steel (E = 200 GPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³), Al (E = 72 GPa, ρ = 2,800 kg/m³), Ti (E = 110 GPa, ρ = 4,430 kg/m³) and CFRP along the fibres (E = 135 GPa, ρ = 1,600 kg/m³). Which statement about specific stiffness (E/ρ) is correct?
options: Steel has the largest E, so its specific stiffness is also the highest
Al's specific stiffness is about 3 times that of steel
Ti's specific stiffness is higher than CFRP's
All three metals are at about 25 MN·m/kg, while CFRP is at about 84 MN·m/kg
aero-w10-q4.explanation: Steel 200/7.85 ≈ 25.5, Al 72/2.8 ≈ 25.7, Ti 110/4.43 ≈ 24.8 MN·m/kg, so the three metals are about equal. CFRP 135/1.6 ≈ 84.4 MN·m/kg. Trap: looking only at E and putting steel ahead; its density is just as much higher. Al's E is about 3 times lower than steel's, not its specific stiffness 3 times higher.

aero-w10-q5.question: A tension member is made of aluminium (σ_allow = 500 MPa, ρ = 2,800 kg/m³) and has a mass of 12 kg. If it is made of titanium (σ_allow = 900 MPa, ρ = 4,430 kg/m³) for the same load and length (area = load/σ_allow), what is the new mass?
aero-w10-q5.explanation: For the same load, area ∝ 1/σ, and mass = ρ × area × length, so mass ∝ ρ/σ. New mass = 12 × (4,430/900)/(2,800/500) = 12 × 4.922/5.6 ≈ 10.5 kg. Trap: using only the density ratio gives 19.0 kg, and only the strength ratio gives 6.67 kg; both apply together.

aero-w10-q6.question: A fitting has run 30,000 cycles at a stress level where its fatigue life is 150,000 cycles, and 8,000 cycles at a higher stress level where its life is 20,000 cycles. By Miner's rule (D = Σ n/N, failure at D = 1), how many more cycles can it run at the higher stress level?
aero-w10-q6.explanation: Damage so far = 30,000/150,000 + 8,000/20,000 = 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6. Damage left = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4. Cycles at the higher stress = 0.4 × 20,000 = 8,000. Trap: treating the used damage 0.6 as what is left gives 12,000, ignoring the earlier cycles gives 20,000, and multiplying by the low-stress life (150,000) gives 60,000.

aero-w10-q7.question: What does it mean that CFRP is "anisotropic"?
options: It has the same strength in every direction
aero-w10-q7.explanation: Anisotropic means strong along the fibres and weak across them, so layers are laid at different angles. Trap: the same property in every direction describes an isotropic material (like metals); corrosion and temperature are separate properties.

aero-w10-q8.question: Which aluminium alloy series is usually used in the lower wing skin and fuselage, where fatigue and damage tolerance matter most?
aero-w10-q8.explanation: The 2xxx series (2024) gives good fatigue and damage tolerance, so it is used in the lower wing skin and fuselage. Trap: 7xxx (7075) is for high strength in the upper wing, and steel or titanium are not aluminium alloy series.

aero-w10-q9.question: Why are titanium alloys used instead of aluminium near the hot parts of an engine?
options: Titanium keeps its strength at higher temperatures
Titanium has much higher stiffness per kg
aero-w10-q9.explanation: Aluminium loses strength above about 150 °C, while titanium offers high-temperature capability and corrosion resistance. Trap: titanium is heavier than aluminium, expensive and hard to machine, and its E/ρ is about the same as aluminium's.

aero-w10-q10.question: A fitting has run 40,000 cycles at a stress where its fatigue life is 200,000 cycles, and 5,000 cycles at a stress where its life is 25,000 cycles. Using Miner's rule, what is the cumulative damage D so far?
aero-w10-q10.explanation: D = 40,000/200,000 + 5,000/25,000 = 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.40, so 40% of the life is used up. Trap: counting only one level gives 0.20, inverting D (1/D) gives 2.5, and a misplaced decimal gives 0.04.

aero-w10-q11.question: A stiffness-limited tension member (area = load/(E × allowed strain)) made of aluminium (E = 72 GPa, ρ = 2,800 kg/m³) has a mass of 10 kg. For the same stiffness and length, what would its mass be in CFRP along the fibres (E = 135 GPa, ρ = 1,600 kg/m³)?
aero-w10-q11.explanation: Mass ∝ ρ/E. CFRP: 1,600/135 = 11.85; Al: 2,800/72 = 38.89. New mass = 10 × 11.85/38.89 ≈ 3.05 kg. Trap: using only the density ratio gives 5.71 kg, inverting the ratio gives 32.8 kg, and comparing by strength (σ/ρ) gives 1.90 kg, which is the wrong basis for a stiffness-limited part.

aero-w10-q12.question: Each flight, a fuselage panel sees 1 pressurisation cycle (fatigue life 60,000 cycles) and 10 gust cycles (fatigue life 2,000,000 cycles). Using Miner's rule, after about how many flights will D = 1?
aero-w10-q12.explanation: Damage per flight D = 1/60,000 + 10/2,000,000 = 1.667 × 10⁻⁵ + 0.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 2.167 × 10⁻⁵. Flights = 1/(2.167 × 10⁻⁵) ≈ 46,200. Trap: ignoring the gusts gives 60,000, looking only at the gusts gives 200,000, and dividing the pressurisation life by the 10 gust cycles gives 6,000.

aero-w10-q13.question: A strength-limited tension member made of aluminium (σ = 500 MPa, ρ = 2,800 kg/m³) has a mass of 12 kg. CFRP (ρ = 1,600 kg/m³) has a strength of 1,500 MPa along the fibres but only 50 MPa across them. If by mistake the fibres are laid across the load, what is the mass of the CFRP member for the same load and length? (area = load/σ)
aero-w10-q13.explanation: Mass ∝ ρ/σ. Across the fibres: 1,600/50 = 32; Al: 2,800/500 = 5.6. Mass = 12 × 32/5.6 ≈ 68.6 kg. Along the fibres it would be only 12 × (1,600/1,500)/5.6 ≈ 2.29 kg. Trap: using the fibre-direction strength gives 2.29 kg (anisotropy forgotten), treating the materials as equal gives 12.0 kg, and a misplaced decimal gives 6.86 kg.

aero-w10-q14.question: Compare high-strength steel (σ = 1,800 MPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³) and a Ti alloy (σ = 900 MPa, ρ = 4,430 kg/m³) for a strength-limited tension member. For the same load and length (area = load/σ), which is lighter?
aero-w10-q14.explanation: Mass ∝ ρ/σ. Steel: 7,850/1,800 = 4.36; Ti: 4,430/900 = 4.92. Steel/Ti = 0.886, so steel is about 11% lighter; this is why steel is used in compact high-load parts such as landing gear. Trap: looking only at density makes titanium look 44% lighter, and reading the ratio the wrong way makes titanium look 12% lighter.

aero-w10-q15.question: A stiffness-limited panel is made of aluminium (E = 72 GPa, ρ = 2,800 kg/m³). If it is made of a Ti alloy (E = 110 GPa, ρ = 4,430 kg/m³) for the same stiffness (mass ∝ ρ/E), how does the mass change?
aero-w10-q15.explanation: Ti: 4,430/110 = 40.3; Al: 2,800/72 = 38.9. Ratio = 1.036, so Ti is about 4% heavier. This is the same fact that metals have nearly the same E/ρ. Trap: using only the density ratio gives 58% heavier, and thinking in terms of strength (σ/ρ) makes Ti look 12% lighter, which is the wrong basis for a stiffness-limited part.

aero-w11-q1.question: Why does a GEO satellite appear fixed at one spot in the sky from the ground?
options: It circles above the equator, in the direction of Earth's rotation, with a period of one sidereal day
It stops in orbit because gravity is balanced there
It is in a polar orbit that turns with the Earth
It is so far away that gravity becomes zero there
aero-w11-q1.explanation: A GEO satellite's period equals Earth's rotation (23 h 56 min), and it moves in the equatorial plane in the same direction, so it keeps pace with the ground. It is moving at about 3.07 km/s, not standing still. Trap: assuming gravity is zero; there is gravity even at 42,164 km and it is what keeps the satellite in orbit.

aero-w11-q2.question: How does the orbital speed of a satellite in LEO compare with that of a GEO satellite?
options: Lower, because there is a little air drag in LEO
Equal, because all satellites have the same speed
Higher, because r is smaller in v = √(GM/r)
aero-w11-q2.explanation: v = √(GM/r): smaller r ⇒ higher v. About 7.7 km/s in LEO and about 3.1 km/s in GEO. Trap: thinking r is in the numerator and saying 'lower'; drag is not what sets the speed, it only slowly lowers the orbit.

aero-w11-q3.question: A satellite is in a circular orbit at 500 km altitude. Taking GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and R_earth = 6,371 km, what is its orbital speed?
aero-w11-q3.explanation: r = 6,371 + 500 = 6,871 km = 6.871 × 10⁶ m. v = √((3.986 × 10¹⁴)/(6.871 × 10⁶)) ≈ 7,617 m/s ≈ 7.62 km/s. Trap: using only the altitude (500 km) as r gives 28.2 km/s, using just R_earth gives 7.91 km/s, and not converting km to m gives 241 km/s.

aero-w11-q4.question: What is the orbital period of the same satellite (r = 6,871 km, v ≈ 7,617 m/s)?
aero-w11-q4.explanation: T = 2πr/v = 2π × 6.871 × 10⁶/7,617 ≈ 5,668 s ≈ 94.5 min. Trap: forgetting 2π and using r/v gives 15.0 min, using R_earth instead of r gives 87.6 min, and writing the seconds as minutes gives 5,669.

aero-w11-q5.question: A satellite's circular orbit radius (from Earth's centre) is made 4 times larger. By Kepler's third law, how many times longer is its period?
aero-w11-q5.explanation: T² ∝ r³ ⇒ T ∝ r^(3/2). r 4 times ⇒ T = 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 2³ = 8 times. Trap: treating T as proportional to r and saying 4 times, or reading T² ∝ r³ as T ∝ r² and saying 16 times.

aero-w11-q6.question: A spacecraft is in a circular orbit at 400 km altitude (r = 6,771 km, GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²). What minimum extra Δv is needed to escape Earth's gravity from this point (one quick burn along the direction of motion)?
aero-w11-q6.explanation: v_circ = √((3.986 × 10¹⁴)/(6.771 × 10⁶)) ≈ 7.67 km/s. v_esc = √2 × 7.67 ≈ 10.85 km/s. Extra Δv = 10.85 − 7.67 ≈ 3.18 km/s, because the spacecraft is already moving at 7.67 km/s. Trap: taking the full escape speed (10.85) as the Δv, or using the escape speed from the surface (11.19 km/s).

aero-w11-q7.question: Which type of orbit are the GPS navigation satellites in?
aero-w11-q7.explanation: The GPS constellation is in MEO at about 20,200 km. Trap: LEO is for the space station and imaging, GEO for communication and weather, and the sun-synchronous orbit for Earth observation.

aero-w11-q8.question: Why can a rover on Mars not be driven live from Earth with a joystick?
options: Radio does not work on Mars
The signal delay is several minutes
aero-w11-q8.explanation: The signal travels at light speed but still takes several minutes to reach Mars, so the rover needs autonomy to see obstacles and plan its path itself. Trap: radio works out to Mars, rovers carry cameras, and Mars gravity is lower than Earth's.

aero-w11-q9.question: What is a geosynchronous transfer orbit (GTO)?
options: A polar LEO that passes every place at the same solar time
A path that escapes Earth gravity towards the Moon
A circular 400 km parking orbit above the equator
An elliptical orbit where the launcher releases a GEO satellite
aero-w11-q9.explanation: A GTO is an elliptical orbit in which the launch vehicle releases GEO satellites; the satellite later uses its own engine to reach circular GEO. Trap: the polar same-solar-time orbit is sun-synchronous, and a GTO is neither an escape path nor a circular LEO.

aero-w11-q10.question: A satellite is in a circular orbit at 6.0 km/s. What speed is needed to escape Earth's gravity from that same radius?
aero-w11-q10.explanation: v_esc = √2 × v_circular = 1.414 × 6.0 ≈ 8.49 km/s. Trap: multiplying by 2 gives 12.0 km/s, dividing by √2 gives 4.24 km/s, and 11.2 km/s is the escape speed from Earth's surface only, not from this radius.

aero-w11-q11.question: The Moon is about 384,400 km away. What is the minimum time to send a command to a rover from Earth and see its response (a camera image) back? (c = 3 × 10⁵ km/s)
aero-w11-q11.explanation: One-way = 384,400/300,000 ≈ 1.28 s. Command out + response back = 2 × 1.28 ≈ 2.56 s. Trap: taking only one way gives 1.28 s, halving gives 0.64 s, and counting the legs twice gives 5.13 s.

aero-w11-q12.question: A navigation satellite is in a circular orbit at an altitude of 20,200 km. Taking R_earth = 6,371 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², what is its period?
aero-w11-q12.explanation: r = 6,371 + 20,200 = 26,571 km = 2.6571 × 10⁷ m. T = 2π√(r³/GM) = 2π√(1.876 × 10²²/3.986 × 10¹⁴) ≈ 43,100 s ≈ 11.97 h (about half a day). Trap: using only the altitude as r gives 7.94 h, treating it like GEO with a one-day period gives 23.9 h, and forgetting the 2π gives 1.91 h.

aero-w11-q13.question: An imaging satellite needs a period of exactly 100 min. Taking GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and R_earth = 6,371 km, what is the altitude of the circular orbit?
aero-w11-q13.explanation: T = 6,000 s. r³ = GM T²/(4π²) = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ × 3.6 × 10⁷/39.48 ≈ 3.635 × 10²⁰, so r ≈ 7.137 × 10⁶ m = 7,137 km. Altitude = 7,137 − 6,371 ≈ 766 km. Trap: forgetting to subtract R_earth gives 7,137 km (that is the radius), and forgetting to divide by 4π² gives about 17,900 km.

aero-w11-q14.question: At one time Mars is 2.25 × 10⁸ km from Earth (c = 3 × 10⁵ km/s). A rover moves at 4 cm/s. As soon as the operator on Earth sees an obstacle in the rover's image, they send "stop". From when the image was taken to when the stop command arrives, how far has the rover moved?
aero-w11-q14.explanation: One-way delay = 2.25 × 10⁸/(3 × 10⁵) = 750 s. The image takes 750 s to arrive and the stop takes 750 s to get there, 1,500 s in total. Distance = 0.04 × 1,500 = 60 m. This is why the rover needs autonomy to stop by itself. Trap: taking only one leg gives 30 m, a wrong cm-to-m conversion gives a huge number like 3.6 km, and using the delay in minutes (25 min) instead of seconds gives 1 m.

aero-w11-q15.question: A LEO satellite has a period of 92 min and a GEO satellite 1,436 min. Using Kepler's third law (T² ∝ r³), the GEO orbit radius is about how many times the LEO radius?
aero-w11-q15.explanation: Period ratio = 1,436/92 ≈ 15.6. r ∝ T^(2/3), so the radius ratio = 15.6^(2/3) ≈ 6.25 (check: 42,164/6,771 ≈ 6.23). Trap: taking the period ratio as the radius ratio gives 15.6, taking the square root gives 3.95, and using the power 3/2 gives 61.7.

aero-w12-q1.question: Which of these is a security issue rather than a safety issue?
options: A mistake by a tired pilot
Someone deliberately spoofing the GPS signal
A metal fatigue crack in the fuselage
aero-w12-q1.explanation: Security deals with deliberate harm; GPS spoofing is an intentional attack. A bird strike, a fatigue-related mistake and metal fatigue are all unintentional hazards, so they are safety issues. Trap: being confused because the word 'fatigue' appears in two options.

aero-w12-q2.question: What is the main aim of an aircraft accident investigation?
options: Finding the person responsible and getting them punished
Understanding the cause so that similar accidents do not happen again
Deciding the amount of the airline's insurance claim
aero-w12-q2.explanation: In international practice the purpose of a safety investigation is prevention: understanding what happened and why, and making safety recommendations. Blame and liability are separate processes. Trap: taking the focus on blame in the news as the aim of the investigation.

aero-w12-q3.question: An aircraft has three independent hydraulic systems. Each has a probability of 10⁻⁴ of failing in a flight hour. What is the probability that all three fail together?
aero-w12-q3.explanation: For independent events, P(all three fail) = 10⁻⁴ × 10⁻⁴ × 10⁻⁴ = 10⁻¹². Trap: adding the probabilities gives 3 × 10⁻⁴ (that is roughly the chance that at least one fails), and using only two systems gives 10⁻⁸.

aero-w12-q4.question: A navigation chain has 4 components in series (all must work). Each component has a reliability of 0.98. What is the reliability of the whole chain?
aero-w12-q4.explanation: Series system: R = 0.98⁴ = 0.98 × 0.98 × 0.98 × 0.98 ≈ 0.922. Every extra series component lowers reliability. Trap: 0.99999984 is the answer for a parallel system (1 − 0.02⁴), and 3.92 comes from adding reliabilities, which is impossible since it exceeds 1.

aero-w12-q5.question: Three identical flight computers run exactly the same software. Which kind of failure can this triple redundancy not protect against?
options: The power supply of one computer failing
A random hardware fault in one computer's chip
A software bug that triggers in all three on the same input (common-mode failure)
A loose connector on one computer
aero-w12-q5.explanation: A bug in identical software appears in all three computers at once on the same input, so voting finds all three wrong; this is a common-mode failure. A random fault in one computer is outvoted by the other two. That is why critical systems use dissimilar software and hardware. Trap: assuming three copies protect against every failure.

aero-w12-q6.question: A triplex sensor system uses 2-out-of-3 voting (at least two sensors must be correct). Each sensor has a reliability of 0.95 and the sensors are independent. What is the system reliability?
aero-w12-q6.explanation: R = 3r² − 2r³ = 3 × 0.9025 − 2 × 0.857375 = 2.7075 − 1.71475 ≈ 0.993. Trap: 0.857 = 0.95³ (all three must be correct), and 0.999875 = 1 − 0.05³ (any one is enough), which is not the condition for a voting system.

aero-w12-q7.question: Who is the civil aviation regulator in India?
aero-w12-q7.explanation: The DGCA is India's civil aviation regulator. Trap: ICAO sets international standards, the AAIB investigates accidents, and ISRO is the space agency, not a regulator.

aero-w12-q8.question: What does the Swiss cheese model say about accidents?
options: Every accident comes from one single pilot error
Adding more defence layers actually lowers safety
Accidents come only from technical failure, not people
An accident happens when holes in several layers line up
aero-w12-q8.explanation: Every layer (design, maintenance, training, procedures, ATC) has some weaknesses; an accident happens when holes in several layers line up, so there are usually several factors. Trap: the model is the opposite of the single-error or technical-failure-only view.

aero-w12-q9.question: What is the main idea of Crew Resource Management (CRM)?
options: Only the captain makes every decision alone
Crew members challenge each other and share tasks
Keeping automation fully switched off always
Relying only on memory instead of checklists
aero-w12-q9.explanation: In CRM the crew challenge each other and share tasks to catch human errors. Trap: leaving all decisions to the captain or dropping checklists goes against CRM, and automation should be used sensibly, not switched off.

aero-w12-q10.question: A function runs on two independent channels and either one working is enough. Each channel has reliability 0.95. What is the system reliability?
aero-w12-q10.explanation: Parallel: R = 1 − (1 − 0.95)² = 1 − 0.0025 = 0.9975. Trap: multiplying as for series gives 0.9025 (the chance both work), ignoring the redundancy gives 0.95, and adding the reliabilities gives 1.90, which cannot be a probability.

aero-w12-q11.question: What is the difference between a type certificate and a certificate of airworthiness?
options: They are the same document with different names
The type certificate covers the design, airworthiness each aircraft
A type certificate is issued before every flight
A certificate of airworthiness is given only to the pilot
aero-w12-q11.explanation: A type certificate is issued when the regulator accepts that the design meets the airworthiness standards. Each individual aircraft needs its own certificate of airworthiness and regular maintenance. Trap: they are two separate documents, not issued per flight, and a pilot's licence is a different thing.

aero-w12-q12.question: A hydraulic line has two independent pumps in parallel (either is enough, each with reliability 0.9), followed by a valve in series (reliability 0.99). What is the reliability of the whole line?
aero-w12-q12.explanation: Pumps in parallel: 1 − (0.1)² = 0.99. Valve in series: 0.99 × 0.99 ≈ 0.980. Trap: treating everything as series gives 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.99 ≈ 0.802, using just one pump gives 0.891, and forgetting the valve gives 0.990.

aero-w12-q13.question: Each sensor has reliability r = 0.9 and the sensors are independent. Order these three designs by reliability: a single sensor, duplex (any 1 of 2 is enough), and triplex 2-out-of-3 voting.
aero-w12-q13.explanation: Single = 0.900. Duplex parallel = 1 − 0.1² = 0.990. 2-out-of-3 = 3r² − 2r³ = 2.43 − 1.458 = 0.972. So duplex > 2-out-of-3 > single; voting gives up a little reliability but catches a sensor giving wrong output. Trap: taking 2-out-of-3 as 1 − 0.1³ = 0.999 (the any-one-is-enough formula), and treating parallel like series as r² = 0.810.

aero-w12-q14.question: Each of three independent flight computers has a failure probability of 10⁻³ per flight (any one is enough). But all three run on a single power supply with failure probability 10⁻⁵. What is the system failure probability, roughly?
aero-w12-q14.explanation: All three computers failing together: (10⁻³)³ = 10⁻⁹. The power supply is in series, so failure ≈ 10⁻⁹ + 10⁻⁵ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. The common-mode power supply dominates. Trap: forgetting the power supply gives 10⁻⁹, adding the computer failure probabilities gives 3 × 10⁻³, and multiplying 10⁻⁹ by 10⁻⁵ gives 10⁻¹⁴.

aero-w12-q15.question: An airline's operation sees 1,000 hazard events a year. Four independent defence layers fail to catch a hazard with probabilities 0.1, 0.05, 0.2 and 0.02. An accident happens only if all four layers miss. How many accidents are expected per year?
aero-w12-q15.explanation: Probability that all four layers miss = 0.1 × 0.05 × 0.2 × 0.02 = 2 × 10⁻⁵. Expected accidents = 1,000 × 2 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.02 per year, about one in 50 years. This is the Swiss cheese model in numbers. Trap: adding the probabilities gives 370, and slipping a power or two of 10 in the multiplication gives 20 or 0.2.
